# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
Don’t dismiss Mexico City’s ritziest neighborhood — it’s got a lot to offer
byDaniela Galarza
Mar 21, 2016, 1:30 PM UTC
*
It’s easy to dismiss Polanco — the Beverly Hills of Mexico City — as a skippable part of town overrun by politicos, their cronies, very wealthy locals, and very wealthy tourists. Still, it’s likely you’ll end up here for one reason or another: The city’s fanciest hotels stand in this area, and so are some of its most highly-rated restaurants. Unfortunately, they share space with American-import chain restaurants, tourist-trap quasi-European wine bars, and Starbucks. Steer clear of those options and consider these far better picks.
See guides to all of Mexico City’s greatest neighborhoods — plus everything you need to know about eating in DF, one of the best food cities in the world — in the **Eater Guide to Mexico City.**

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
Don’t dismiss Mexico City’s ritziest neighborhood — it’s got a lot to offer
byDaniela Galarza
Mar 21, 2016, 1:30 PM UTC
*
It’s easy to dismiss Polanco — the Beverly Hills of Mexico City — as a skippable part of town overrun by politicos, their cronies, very wealthy locals, and very wealthy tourists. Still, it’s likely you’ll end up here for one reason or another: The city’s fanciest hotels stand in this area, and so are some of its most highly-rated restaurants. Unfortunately, they share space with American-import chain restaurants, tourist-trap quasi-European wine bars, and Starbucks. Steer clear of those options and consider these far better picks.
See guides to all of Mexico City’s greatest neighborhoods — plus everything you need to know about eating in DF, one of the best food cities in the world — in the **Eater Guide to Mexico City.**

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## Maque Café
Part of a small chain of cozy bakeries, the here pastries are serviceable. But dine at a table for the full cafe menu, which includes huevos rancheros served with warm, soupy black beans.
Loved it Want to try
*   Emilio Castelar 209, Miguel Hidalgo, Mexico City 11560, Mexico  
*   [+52 55 2489 5695](tel:525524895695)  
*   Visit Website

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## El Turix
One of the best taquerias in the city looks completely out of place just steps from DF’s Louis Vuitton, but it’s one of the main reasons food enthusiasts will visit this part of town (if they’re not staying nearby already). Get anything with the house _cochinita pibil_, a style of slow-roasted pork from the Yucatán.
Loved it Want to try
*   Emilio Castelar 212, Miguel Hidalgo, Distrito Federa, Mexico  
*   [+52 55 5280 6449](tel:525552806449)

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## Pujol
Enrique Olvera’s fine dining restaurant is world-famous for a reason: it serves really fantastic food. Get a little dressed up for the elegant dinnertime tasting menu, or try for a more casual lunch, provided you plan ahead and score a reservation. Try calling at the last minute for late afternoon tables, which are sometimes easier to get than prime times.
Loved it Want to try
*   Francisco Petrarca 254, Miguel Hidalgo, Mexico City 11570, Mexico  
*   [+52 55 5545 4111](tel:525555454111)  
*   Visit Website

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## Quintonil
Chef Jorge Vallejo and his wife Alejandra Flores are behind this, Mexico City’s current fine dining mecca. That Vallejo trained under Olvera at Pujol, and has something to prove, is something you might hear whispered in the dining room. So far, the critics and the people love it. Consider the a la carte menu for lunch.
Loved it Want to try
*   Newton 55, Polanco, Mexico City, Mexico  
*   [+52 55 5280 2680](tel:525552802680)  
*   Visit Website

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## Dulce Patria
Chef Martha Ortiz just snagged a spot on the new Top Chef Mexico; her dramatic flair and feminist ideals will likely be a welcome addition to this franchise of the Bravo show. Her restaurant draws an unsurprisingly hip clientele, and the dining room’s decoration — scarlet, white, and fuchsia — hints at the dishes to come. Ortiz’s food is romantic, but bold and completely unexpected.
Loved it Want to try
*   Anatole France 100, Mexico City, Mexico City 11560, Mexico  
*   [+52 55 3300 3999](tel:525533003999)  
*   Visit Website

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## Jules Basement
You’ll never find this place unless someone tells you where it is. Hidden behind what looks like the door to a walk-in cooler inside a basic cantina is one of this part of town’s coolest bars. It’s not new, but the speakeasy-style is fun and the drinks are grand.
Loved it Want to try
*   Julio Verne, Mexico City, Mexico City, Mexico  
*   Visit Website

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## Amado
What could easily have been an overwrought and overly sweet hotel bakery inside the Hyatt Regency is, happily, a fine _pastelería_ and _panadería_. It’s comfortable, serves excellent coffee, and displays dozens of flavorful, nuanced baked goods that borrow heavily from European technique.
Loved it Want to try
*   Campos Eliseos 204, Mexico, Mexico

## Amado

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## El Chapulín
This restaurant inside the Hotel Intercontinental pays homage to Mexico’s indigenous cuisine but also offers excellent modern standards, including tacos, shellfish from Baja, and rice and beans. The service is good and the prices are fair, especially considering the location.
Loved it Want to try
*   Campos Elíseos #218, Bosques de Chapultepec (Polanco), Mexico City, Mexico City 11580, Mexico  
*   Visit Website

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## Guzina Oaxaca
Though the menu is authentic and the service friendly, this upscale Oaxacan spot attracts more tourists than locals. Still, the moles are fantastic and tortillas freshly made and plentiful.
Loved it Want to try
*   Masaryk 513, Mexico City, Mexico City 11530, Mexico  
*   [+52 55 5282 1820](tel:525552821820)  
*   Visit Website

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## eno
Here, chef Enrique Olvera (yes, the same man behind Pujol) gets to play with casual cafe food. While the results are not quite as mind-blowing as the things he gets up to in his fine dining establishment, the baked goods and coffee are top notch.
Loved it Want to try
*   Francisco Petrarca 258, Miguel Hidalgo, Mexico City, Mexico  
*   [+52 55 5531 8535](tel:525555318535)

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
Don’t dismiss Mexico City’s ritziest neighborhood — it’s got a lot to offer
byDaniela Galarza
Mar 21, 2016, 1:30 PM UTC
*
It’s easy to dismiss Polanco — the Beverly Hills of Mexico City — as a skippable part of town overrun by politicos, their cronies, very wealthy locals, and very wealthy tourists. Still, it’s likely you’ll end up here for one reason or another: The city’s fanciest hotels stand in this area, and so are some of its most highly-rated restaurants. Unfortunately, they share space with American-import chain restaurants, tourist-trap quasi-European wine bars, and Starbucks. Steer clear of those options and consider these far better picks.
See guides to all of Mexico City’s greatest neighborhoods — plus everything you need to know about eating in DF, one of the best food cities in the world — in the **Eater Guide to Mexico City.**

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## Maque Café
Part of a small chain of cozy bakeries, the here pastries are serviceable. But dine at a table for the full cafe menu, which includes huevos rancheros served with warm, soupy black beans.
Loved it Want to try
*   Emilio Castelar 209, Miguel Hidalgo, Mexico City 11560, Mexico  
*   [+52 55 2489 5695](tel:525524895695)  
*   Visit Website
texts.5:
# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## El Turix
One of the best taquerias in the city looks completely out of place just steps from DF’s Louis Vuitton, but it’s one of the main reasons food enthusiasts will visit this part of town (if they’re not staying nearby already). Get anything with the house _cochinita pibil_, a style of slow-roasted pork from the Yucatán.
Loved it Want to try
*   Emilio Castelar 212, Miguel Hidalgo, Distrito Federa, Mexico  
*   [+52 55 5280 6449](tel:525552806449)
texts.6:
# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## Pujol
Enrique Olvera’s fine dining restaurant is world-famous for a reason: it serves really fantastic food. Get a little dressed up for the elegant dinnertime tasting menu, or try for a more casual lunch, provided you plan ahead and score a reservation. Try calling at the last minute for late afternoon tables, which are sometimes easier to get than prime times.
Loved it Want to try
*   Francisco Petrarca 254, Miguel Hidalgo, Mexico City 11570, Mexico  
*   [+52 55 5545 4111](tel:525555454111)  
*   Visit Website
texts.7:
# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## Quintonil
Chef Jorge Vallejo and his wife Alejandra Flores are behind this, Mexico City’s current fine dining mecca. That Vallejo trained under Olvera at Pujol, and has something to prove, is something you might hear whispered in the dining room. So far, the critics and the people love it. Consider the a la carte menu for lunch.
Loved it Want to try
*   Newton 55, Polanco, Mexico City, Mexico  
*   [+52 55 5280 2680](tel:525552802680)  
*   Visit Website
texts.8:
# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## Dulce Patria
Chef Martha Ortiz just snagged a spot on the new Top Chef Mexico; her dramatic flair and feminist ideals will likely be a welcome addition to this franchise of the Bravo show. Her restaurant draws an unsurprisingly hip clientele, and the dining room’s decoration — scarlet, white, and fuchsia — hints at the dishes to come. Ortiz’s food is romantic, but bold and completely unexpected.
Loved it Want to try
*   Anatole France 100, Mexico City, Mexico City 11560, Mexico  
*   [+52 55 3300 3999](tel:525533003999)  
*   Visit Website
texts.9:
# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## Jules Basement
You’ll never find this place unless someone tells you where it is. Hidden behind what looks like the door to a walk-in cooler inside a basic cantina is one of this part of town’s coolest bars. It’s not new, but the speakeasy-style is fun and the drinks are grand.
Loved it Want to try
*   Julio Verne, Mexico City, Mexico City, Mexico  
*   Visit Website
texts.10:
# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## Amado
What could easily have been an overwrought and overly sweet hotel bakery inside the Hyatt Regency is, happily, a fine _pastelería_ and _panadería_. It’s comfortable, serves excellent coffee, and displays dozens of flavorful, nuanced baked goods that borrow heavily from European technique.
Loved it Want to try
*   Campos Eliseos 204, Mexico, Mexico

This restaurant inside the Hotel Intercontinental pays homage to Mexico’s indigenous cuisine but also offers excellent modern standards, including tacos, shellfish from Baja, and rice and beans. The service is good and the prices are fair, especially considering the location.

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## Guzina Oaxaca
Though the menu is authentic and the service friendly, this upscale Oaxacan spot attracts more tourists than locals. Still, the moles are fantastic and tortillas freshly made and plentiful.

Polanco is one of Mexico City’s most upscale neighbourhoods, known for designer shopping, high-end restaurants and some excellent museums. But you don’t need a luxury budget to enjoy it. If you’re wondering what to do in Polanco, Mexico City, the free art museums, bookshop cafés and a stroll around Parque Lincoln make a worthwhile half-day, even if shopping isn’t your thing.
Video 5  
Video Muted
We keep coming back for the art, having visited Museo Soumaya and Museo Jumex more than once, usually with coffee and cake afterwards. This guide covers those favourites alongside shopping spots, parks and places we’ve eaten, including the food tour we took. We’ll also help you plan a walking route between the museum district in Nuevo Polanco and the older streets around Masaryk and Parque Lincoln.

## Quick Guide to Polanco
**Best for:** art museums, shopping, café stops and upscale dining
**Where to explore:** Nuevo Polanco for Soumaya and Jumex; Masaryk and Parque Lincoln for shopping, cafés and leafy streets
**How long to spend:** half a day for selected highlights; a full day for both museums, shopping and a leisurely lunch
**Getting here:** Uber is convenient; choose your drop-off near Soumaya/Jumex or Parque Lincoln, depending on where you want to start
**Getting around:** explore on foot, but allow time to walk between the museum district and the streets around Parque Lincoln
**Is Polanco worth visiting?** Yes, even if you don’t shop, the **free museums** (Soumaya + Jumex) make it one of the best half-day trips in Mexico City.
**What’s Polanco best known for?** Luxury shopping (Masaryk), modern museums, and high-end dining, plus it’s one of the easiest CDMX neighborhoods to walk around.

## A Half-Day Walking Route Through Polanco
Start at **Museo Jumex**, see the exhibitions and stop for coffee and cake downstairs, as we usually do. Then visit **Museo Soumaya** next door. If you want a shorter outing, choose whichever museum interests you most rather than rushing through both.
Tap or click the map to open the walking route in Google Maps, with exact stop locations and directions.
From the museums, head south towards **Avenida Presidente Masaryk**. Shopping enthusiasts can detour through **Antara** or **Palacio de Hierro** along the way, but they’re optional stops.
Follow Masaryk towards **Pasaje Polanco**, the pretty shopping courtyard where I bought a dress, then take a break in **Parque Lincoln**. Finish with cochinita pibil tacos at **El Turix**, or head to **El Péndulo** if you’d prefer a sit-down meal in a bookshop café.
Route: Jumex → Soumaya → optional Antara and Palacio de Hierro → Masaryk → Pasaje Polanco → optional El Péndulo → Parque Lincoln → El Turix.
Allow **half a day for selected stops**, or longer if you visit both museums and spend time shopping. The museums are in Nuevo Polanco, so this includes a walk between two distinct parts of the neighbourhood. Save Anthropology and Chapultepec for a separate outing if you want to explore them properly.

## **Polanco Map: Our Saved Pins**
We’ve pinned the museums, shopping spots, parks and places to eat mentioned in this guide, so you can choose your own stops.
Tap or click the map to open all our saved locations in Google Maps.
One of the nicest places to stay in CDMX, Polanco was **extensively developed in the 1930s** to create an upmarket residential district for the increasingly wealthy middle classes. It’s been a hub of affluence ever since, blending ornate mansions with luxe apartment blocks.
Everything in this part of town **feels just a little more sophisticated**, including the local parks where residents go to walk their dogs and exercise their children. It says a lot about Polanco that the **Parque Lincoln**, built during the initial housing boom, has its own aviary!
TOP POLANCO TOUR
**Polanco Food Tour, We Took**
An exciting and delicious  way to explore Polanco! Along with visiting the best dining spots, our guide shared fascinating stories about the neighborhood + local top places to eat. Here is the exact food tour we took:
Just north of traditional Polanco, Nuevo Polanco has developed into a district of modern museums, shopping centres and high-rise buildings. This is where you’ll find Soumaya and Jumex, while the older neighbourhood around Masaryk and Parque Lincoln has the leafy streets, cafés and boutiques. You can explore both on foot, as our walking route above shows.
At the same time, numerous luxury shopping malls and high-end fashion streets have flooded the district, giving rise to Polanco’s nickname as the **‘Beverly Hills of Mexico City.’**It’s also a **fine-dining destination**, home to both Pujol and Quintonil, which each received two Michelin stars in Mexico’s first Michelin guide.
We won't send you spam. Unsubscribe at any time.

## Best Places To Stay In Polanco
Polanco is one of the nicest areas to base yourself in Mexico City if you want a polished, safe-feeling neighbourhood with museums, parks, and great dining on your doorstep — but it’s also one of the pricier places to stay.
If you’re deciding between a leafy, café-heavy base and a more upscale one, our **Condesa vs Polanco** + **Roma Norte vs Polanco** comparisons help.
Want the _“Polanco within Polanco”_ breakdown (Chapultepec/Auditorio vs Masaryk/Parque Lincoln vs Nuevo Polanco) + more hotel options? Start here: **Where to Stay in Polanco**.
top Pick
**The Alest Hotel**
With only 19 rooms, The Alest Hotel is the perfect place to stay in Polanco for style, top-notch facilities and a highly personalised experience.
MIDRANGE Pick
**UTOPIC Palacio Polanco By ULIV**
A different take on Mexico City hotels in Polanco, the UTOPIC Palacio provides**modern studio flats with their own kitchen**facilities that are ideal for people who want to self-cater.

## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
With excellent museums, designer boutiques, and even a renowned hole-in-the-wall taco place, there’s a lot to do in posh Polanco. Here are our top recommendations to add to the itinerary.

## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #1 See Masterpieces At Soumaya Museum
If you do one classic Polanco activity, make it **Museo Soumaya**. We’ve visited more than once, and it’s one of the best things to do in Polanco, Mexico City, for art lovers, with free admission making it an easy addition to your itinerary.
Inside, the collection spans Mexican and European art, with a particular highlight being its extensive collection of **Auguste Rodin sculptures**, one of the largest outside France. The museum was founded by Carlos Slim and named in honour of his late wife, Soumaya. Its glittering exterior is worth seeing even if you don’t venture inside.
Our tip, learned the hard way: weekends can mean queues. We’ve waited outside in full sun before, so aim for a weekday if your schedule allows.
*   **TICKETS:** Free  
*   **OPENING HOURS:** Daily, 10:30 am–6:30 pm

## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #2 Explore Contemporary Art at Museo Jumex (and Grab Coffee Downstairs)
Next door to Soumaya, Museo Jumex is an easy companion stop, particularly if you prefer contemporary art. It’s smaller and more focused, and we’ve visited more than once for its changing exhibitions.
One of our visits was for the **Damien Hirst exhibition**, which we found very thought-provoking. Check the museum’s current programme before visiting to see what interests you. The changing programme is also what makes Jumex worth returning to.
We usually follow our visit with **coffee and cake at the café downstairs**, before continuing around Polanco. Art followed by cake is a routine we’re happy to stick with.
*   **TICKETS:** Free, no reservation needed  
*   **OPENING HOURS:** Tuesday–Friday and Sunday, 10 am–5 pm; Saturday, 10 am–7 pm. **Closed Mondays.**

## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #3 Eat Your Way Around Polanco On A Food Tour
One of the easiest (and most fun) ways to get a feel for Polanco Mexico City is to do a**food tour**. We’ve done a bunch of food tours in CDMX, and this one is a great mix of eating and exploring, you’re not just hopping restaurant to restaurant, you’re also getting context on the neighbourhood as you go.
On the tour we took, we covered multiple stops in just a few hours, with a guide who pointed out iconic buildings and shared little bits of Polanco history between mouthfuls of tacos, mole, and aguas frescas. It was well paced (savoury first, sweet at the end), and it’s a solid option if you want to try several places without overplanning.

## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #4 Go Shopping in Polanco
Polanco is one of Mexico City’s best-known shopping districts, but where you go depends on what you’re looking for: designer boutiques, international brands or smaller fashion shops. These are the four places we’d focus on, even if you’re only window shopping.
Antara

## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #4 Go Shopping in Polanco
#### Avenida Presidente Masaryk: Designer Boutiques
**Masaryk is the main luxury shopping street**, lined with designer storefronts. Start around Pasaje Polanco and explore from there, combining window shopping with the cafés and streets around Parque Lincoln. You don’t need to walk the entire avenue to get a feel for it.

## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #4 Go Shopping in Polanco
#### Antara Fashion Hall: Open-Air Mall
For **international brands in a mall setting**, head to Antara, near Soumaya and Jumex. We liked its open-air layout and central fountain, and it felt surprisingly uncrowded when we visited.
It’s a convenient shopping or coffee stop after the museums, particularly if you don’t want to head straight into the older part of the neighbourhood.

## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #4 Go Shopping in Polanco
#### Pasaje Polanco: Smaller Fashion Shops
**Pasaje Polanco is our favourite of these stops for a leisurely browse.** The neocolonial courtyard feels quite different from the bigger malls, with smaller shops selling women’s fashion. I bought a cute dress here, so our visit went slightly beyond window shopping!
It’s directly on Masaryk and easy to combine with Parque Lincoln and nearby places to eat.

## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #4 Go Shopping in Polanco
#### Palacio de Hierro: Luxury Department Store
For **luxury fashion and beauty counters under one roof**, try Palacio de Hierro. It’s a department store rather than a mall, making it a useful choice if you want to browse indoors or escape the rain.
**Short on time?** Choose Masaryk and Pasaje Polanco for a neighbourhood stroll, or Antara if you’re already visiting the museums. You don’t need to visit all four unless shopping is a priority.

## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #5 Learn About Mesoamerica At The National Museum of Anthropology
Just south of Polanco, in **Chapultepec Park**, the National Museum of Anthropology is one of the most worthwhile museums in Mexico City. It’s a good addition to your visit, but give it its own morning or afternoon rather than squeezing it between Soumaya, Jumex and shopping.
The collection introduces Mexico’s ancient civilisations through extraordinary objects, including **Olmec colossal heads, the Mexica Sun Stone and the jade funerary mask of the Maya ruler Pakal**. These are useful highlights to prioritise if you don’t have time for every gallery.
Allow **at least 2–3 hours for a selective visit**, longer if you enjoy archaeology. Arrive around opening for a quieter start, or book a guided visit if you’d like help understanding the objects and the cultures behind them.
*   **TICKETS:** Check the official INAH listing for current admission prices  
*   **OPENING HOURS:** Tuesday–Sunday, 9 am–6 pm; closed Mondays  
*   **Local tip:** book a guide visit for a more meaningful experience.

## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #6 Get Lost in Chapultepec Park (Castle + Lakes + Museums)
Just south of Polanco, **Chapultepec Park** is a huge green escape with lakes, gardens and museums. It’s worth combining with the neighbourhood, but we’d choose a few stops rather than try to cover the whole park after a morning at Soumaya and Jumex.
On sunny days, we love biking through the park. You can also rent a rowboat on the lake or take a leisurely walk, making this a good option when you’ve had your fill of museum galleries and shopping.
For us, the standout attraction is **Chapultepec Castle**. Commissioned in 1785 as a residence for a Spanish viceroy, it now houses the National Museum of History. Inside, you can explore grand rooms, but our favourite part is the checkerboard terrace and its views across the city.
If you’re visiting Anthropology, you’re already in the park, so combining it with a lakeside walk makes more sense than crossing back and forth between here and Nuevo Polanco.
For more places to explore and practical visiting tips, read our **Chapultepec Park guide**.

## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #7 Try the Tacos at Taquería El Turix
For a casual meal between Polanco’s museums and shopping stops, **Taquería El Turix** is one of our favourites. Its speciality is **cochinita pibil**, slow-cooked pork with citrus and achiote, served in tacos or panuchos.
We tried it on our Polanco food tour, and it’s a great reminder that eating here doesn’t have to involve a tasting menu or a hefty bill. Expect a small, no-frills place where the food does the talking.
There’s no proper seating, so be prepared to eat standing outside or take your order to nearby **Parque Lincoln**. It also makes an easy food stop towards the end of our walking route.
Find more of our favourite taquerías in our guide to **best tacos in Mexico City**.

## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #8 Dine in Style at Pujol (If You’re Planning a Splurge)
Pujol is one of Polanco’s best-known fine-dining restaurants, famous for chef Enrique Olvera’s tasting menus. If a special meal is a priority for your trip, check availability through Pujol’s official website before planning your day around it.
We haven’t eaten here ourselves. We ran out of budget and chose experiences such as the food tour instead, so this is an option to consider rather than a personal dining recommendation.
Check the menu price and what’s included when booking, particularly drinks and any extras. It’s a substantial splurge, but you don’t need a reservation at Pujol to enjoy Polanco: the free museums, parks and casual food stops make a worthwhile visit on their own.

## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #9 Stroll Around Parque Lincoln
Parque Lincoln is the heart of Polanco and one of the nicest places to take a break between museums and shopping. It’s where locals walk their dogs, sit with coffees and bring their kids to play. You don’t need much of an agenda here.
The park has its own aviary, sculptures and two reflecting pools, where we sometimes see people manoeuvring model boats. Those little everyday scenes are part of what we enjoy about wandering around the neighbourhood.
If you’re wondering about the name, the park honours **Abraham Lincoln, who opposed the US invasion of Mexico**. His statue was a gift from President Lyndon Johnson in 1966 and is still on display today.
It’s an easy stop after Pasaje Polanco, with El Turix and several cafés nearby if you’re ready for something to eat.

## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #10 See the Unusual Architecture of St. Augustine Parish Church
A **wonderfully strange, idiosyncratic structure**, the St. Augustine Parish Church was built in 1949 to administer to the spiritual needs of the locals.
Walking towards it from the Parque America, we first thought it looked like a fairly standard religious edifice. As we got closer, though, it became clearer how wonderfully innovative the whole thing is with its almost **industrial-style facade** and a half-dome that has been described by some architecture aficionados as reminiscent of a water tank!

## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #11 Pass Through Parque America
On the way between Old Polanco and Nuevo Polanco, **Parque América** is an easy, pleasant wander, not as iconic as Lincoln, but a nice green break when you’re walking between stops.
We almost always see families here and plenty of dogs, and it’s a good “pause point” before heading back into museums/shopping mode.

## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #12 Take A Photo At Mexico Mi Amor Sign
It might not be on everyone’s list of what to do in Polanco, Mexico City, but getting a snap at the Mexico Mi Amor sign is a fun little **side mission that makes for a stylish Instagram post.**
It’s really a display created by the Tane jewellery store to drum up business, but you don’t have to purchase a diamond-encrusted necklace to take a picture in front of the pinkish-red wall with its green cacti and neon sign.

## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #13 Have Breakfast At El Pendulo Book Store
El Péndulo is one of our favourite **“very CDMX” concepts, a bookstore-meets-café** where you can linger for ages. We usually hang out at the **Condesa** branch, but the Polanco location is just as good, with a terrace that spills onto the street and a cosy, book-lined interior that makes you forget you’re in one of the fanciest parts of the city.
It’s a great stop for breakfast or brunch, especially if you want something more relaxed between museums and shopping. Our usual order is one of the Mexican breakfast plates (their chicken enchiladas in mole are solid), washed down with a big glass of fresh orange juice, plus coffee — and then we inevitably end up browsing books we don’t need.

## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #14 Browse Local Designers at Mercado Escondido (Check Opening Days)
Polanco isn’t really famous for markets, but **Mercado Escondido** is a nice little stop if you’re into local designers, usually a handful of stalls selling things like handmade jewellery, leather goods, and small-batch fashion.
That said, it’s more of a **“nearby bonus stop”** than a must-do, and it can be hit-or-miss depending on the day. We actually showed up once and it was **closed**, so it’s worth checking opening times (or having a backup plan nearby).

## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #15 Read Beside The Lake At Librería Porrúa (Chapultepec)
If you’re doing the Anthropology Museum or spending time in Chapultepec, Librería Porrúa is one of our favourite “slow down” stops. It’s a **bookshop-café with a calm vibe**, perfect for a coffee and a breather after a couple of hours of museums.
If you can, grab a table **beside the lake**. It’s genuinely a lovely place to sit with a drink and decompress, and it feels like a little escape from the city.

## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #16 See the Sharks at Acuario Inbursa (An Option for Families)
If you’re visiting Polanco with kids, **Acuario Inbursa** is another option near Soumaya and Jumex. Its exhibits include sharks, jellyfish and penguins, offering a change from art museums and shopping.
**We haven’t visited ourselves**, so this is an option to consider rather than a personal recommendation. General admission includes both Acuario Inbursa and the Acuario Interactivo; children under three enter free.
If you’re interested in a penguin encounter, check the separate ticket options and availability before booking, as it isn’t included in standard admission.
*   **TICKETS:** $350 MXN general admission, including Acuario Interactivo  
*   **OPENING HOURS:** Daily, 10 am–6 pm  
*   **BOOKING:**Official tickets and current prices

## Is Polanco Safe?
Polanco is one of the **safest-feeling neighborhoods in Mexico City**, where **we’ve felt most comfortable walking around during the day and early evening**. There’s plenty of activity around the shopping streets, restaurants and hotels, and you’ll notice security around many businesses.
That doesn’t mean you should switch off your usual city awareness. We keep bags zipped, avoid leaving phones on café tables and pay attention to our surroundings when checking directions. Late at night, we prefer taking an Uber back rather than walking along quieter streets.
For a broader, city-wide safety breakdown, see our **Mexico City Safety Guide**

## Best Places To Eat In Polanco
Polanco is known for fine dining, but you don’t have to commit to a tasting menu every time you eat here. We’ve found plenty of places for brunch, seafood and tacos, although restaurant prices generally reflect the neighbourhood.
For more recommendations and details, see our **Polanco restaurants guide**.

## Best Places To Eat In Polanco
### Best Brunch & Dinner Spots in Polanco
These are places we’ve enjoyed for a meal without going down the tasting-menu route. They’re not all budget options, but they offer different ways to eat out here.
**Porter Steakhouse & Seafood** – A good choice for a smart dinner without an overly formal atmosphere. We enjoyed the tuna sashimi, and steaks are a main draw if you eat meat.
**Bellopuerto** – One of our go-to picks for seafood. The shrimp aguachile is excellent, but our favourite is the grilled octopus. It’s a good option for sharing a few dishes.
**Catamundi** – Not cheap, but we think it’s worth considering for brunch. The menu includes bagels, shakshuka and Mexican egg dishes, with cocktails if you’re settling in for a long lunch. Our repeat order is the **flautas ahogadas**, crispy tortillas “drowned” in salsa, cheese and cream. There’s also a little gourmet shop attached.

## Best Places To Eat In Polanco
### Best Coffee Shops & Breakfast
For a café break or a relaxed breakfast, these are three places to consider. You’ll find more recommendations in our **best coffee shops in Mexico City** guide.
**Café Toscano Polanco** – An Italian restaurant that also serves Mexican breakfast dishes such as enfrijoladas, enchiladas and molletes. We like the leafy terrace, while the interior has an eclectic mix of furniture and decorative bits.
**Toulo Café** – A café with a Parisian feel and carefully presented cappuccinos, chai lattes and affogatos. Food options include French toast and avocado toast with a poached egg.
**El Péndulo** – Our bookshop-café pick for breakfast and a leisurely browse. We usually order a Mexican breakfast plate, such as chicken enchiladas in mole, with fresh orange juice and coffee.

## Best Places To Eat In Polanco
### Where to Find the Best Tacos in Polanco
For something more casual, these are the taco spots we’ve tried. **El Turix would be our first choice**, particularly if you want cochinita pibil.
**El Turix** – Our favourite for tacos and panuchos filled with cochinita pibil. There’s no proper seating, so eat standing outside or take your order to nearby Parque Lincoln.
**TAKOS TAKOS** – A practical choice when you want a seat and a break from walking. The menu covers everything from salads to meat plates, but we’d stick with the **arrachera tacos**.

## Polanco Nightlife
Polanco nightlife leans towards smart cocktail bars and clubs where people dress up. It’s not our first choice for a big night out, as we prefer **Roma Norte’s** atmosphere, but it’s convenient if you’re staying nearby and want drinks after dinner.
For cocktails, **Licorería Limantour’s Polanco branch**, on Óscar Wilde near Parque Lincoln, is a good option. We still prefer the Roma location for the overall atmosphere, but we’ve enjoyed the drinks here too.
For a club night, **Vanderbilt Masaryk** and **Kennedy Social Room** are options to consider. Expect a dressier evening rather than a casual café-bar atmosphere, and check directly with the venue about reservations, entry arrangements and the night’s programme before heading over.
For more places to go out across the city, read our **Mexico City nightlife guide**.

## Wrap-Up
For us, Polanco is worth visiting for the free museums, a stroll around Masaryk and Parque Lincoln, and a good meal along the way. Choose the stops that interest you rather than trying to cover everything, especially if you’re also planning to visit Chapultepec.
For ideas beyond the neighbourhood, explore our **best things to do in Mexico City**.

## Quick Guide to Polanco
**Best for:** art museums, shopping, café stops and upscale dining
**Where to explore:** Nuevo Polanco for Soumaya and Jumex; Masaryk and Parque Lincoln for shopping, cafés and leafy streets
**How long to spend:** half a day for selected highlights; a full day for both museums, shopping and a leisurely lunch
**Getting here:** Uber is convenient; choose your drop-off near Soumaya/Jumex or Parque Lincoln, depending on where you want to start
**Getting around:** explore on foot, but allow time to walk between the museum district and the streets around Parque Lincoln
**Is Polanco worth visiting?** Yes, even if you don’t shop, the **free museums** (Soumaya + Jumex) make it one of the best half-day trips in Mexico City.
**What’s Polanco best known for?** Luxury shopping (Masaryk), modern museums, and high-end dining, plus it’s one of the easiest CDMX neighborhoods to walk around.

## A Half-Day Walking Route Through Polanco
Start at **Museo Jumex**, see the exhibitions and stop for coffee and cake downstairs, as we usually do. Then visit **Museo Soumaya** next door. If you want a shorter outing, choose whichever museum interests you most rather than rushing through both.
Tap or click the map to open the walking route in Google Maps, with exact stop locations and directions.
From the museums, head south towards **Avenida Presidente Masaryk**. Shopping enthusiasts can detour through **Antara** or **Palacio de Hierro** along the way, but they’re optional stops.
Follow Masaryk towards **Pasaje Polanco**, the pretty shopping courtyard where I bought a dress, then take a break in **Parque Lincoln**. Finish with cochinita pibil tacos at **El Turix**, or head to **El Péndulo** if you’d prefer a sit-down meal in a bookshop café.
Route: Jumex → Soumaya → optional Antara and Palacio de Hierro → Masaryk → Pasaje Polanco → optional El Péndulo → Parque Lincoln → El Turix.
Allow **half a day for selected stops**, or longer if you visit both museums and spend time shopping. The museums are in Nuevo Polanco, so this includes a walk between two distinct parts of the neighbourhood. Save Anthropology and Chapultepec for a separate outing if you want to explore them properly.

One of the nicest places to stay in CDMX, Polanco was **extensively developed in the 1930s** to create an upmarket residential district for the increasingly wealthy middle classes. It’s been a hub of affluence ever since, blending ornate mansions with luxe apartment blocks.
Everything in this part of town **feels just a little more sophisticated**, including the local parks where residents go to walk their dogs and exercise their children. It says a lot about Polanco that the **Parque Lincoln**, built during the initial housing boom, has its own aviary!

Just north of traditional Polanco, Nuevo Polanco has developed into a district of modern museums, shopping centres and high-rise buildings. This is where you’ll find Soumaya and Jumex, while the older neighbourhood around Masaryk and Parque Lincoln has the leafy streets, cafés and boutiques. ## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #1 See Masterpieces At Soumaya Museum
If you do one classic Polanco activity, make it **Museo Soumaya**. We’ve visited more than once, and it’s one of the best things to do in Polanco, Mexico City, for art lovers, with free admission making it an easy addition to your itinerary.
Inside, the collection spans Mexican and European art, with a particular highlight being its extensive collection of **Auguste Rodin sculptures**, one of the largest outside France. The museum was founded by Carlos Slim and named in honour of his late wife, Soumaya. Its glittering exterior is worth seeing even if you don’t venture inside.
Our tip, learned the hard way: weekends can mean queues. We’ve waited outside in full sun before, so aim for a weekday if your schedule allows.
*   **TICKETS:** Free  
*   **OPENING HOURS:** Daily, 10:30 am–6:30 pm

## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #2 Explore Contemporary Art at Museo Jumex (and Grab Coffee Downstairs)
Next door to Soumaya, Museo Jumex is an easy companion stop, particularly if you prefer contemporary art. It’s smaller and more focused, and we’ve visited more than once for its changing exhibitions.
One of our visits was for the **Damien Hirst exhibition**, which we found very thought-provoking. Check the museum’s current programme before visiting to see what interests you. The changing programme is also what makes Jumex worth returning to.
We usually follow our visit with **coffee and cake at the café downstairs**, before continuing around Polanco. Art followed by cake is a routine we’re happy to stick with.
*   **TICKETS:** Free, no reservation needed  
*   **OPENING HOURS:** Tuesday–Friday and Sunday, 10 am–5 pm; Saturday, 10 am–7 pm. **Closed Mondays.**

## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #6 Get Lost in Chapultepec Park (Castle + Lakes + Museums)
Just south of Polanco, **Chapultepec Park** is a huge green escape with lakes, gardens and museums. It’s worth combining with the neighbourhood, but we’d choose a few stops rather than try to cover the whole park after a morning at Soumaya and Jumex.
On sunny days, we love biking through the park. You can also rent a rowboat on the lake or take a leisurely walk, making this a good option when you’ve had your fill of museum galleries and shopping.
For us, the standout attraction is **Chapultepec Castle**. Commissioned in 1785 as a residence for a Spanish viceroy, it now houses the National Museum of History. Inside, you can explore grand rooms, but our favourite part is the checkerboard terrace and its views across the city.
If you’re visiting Anthropology, you’re already in the park, so combining it with a lakeside walk makes more sense than crossing back and forth between here and Nuevo Polanco.
For more places to explore and practical visiting tips, read our **Chapultepec Park guide**.
texts.16:
## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #7 Try the Tacos at Taquería El Turix
For a casual meal between Polanco’s museums and shopping stops, **Taquería El Turix** is one of our favourites. Its speciality is **cochinita pibil**, slow-cooked pork with citrus and achiote, served in tacos or panuchos.
We tried it on our Polanco food tour, and it’s a great reminder that eating here doesn’t have to involve a tasting menu or a hefty bill. Expect a small, no-frills place where the food does the talking.
There’s no proper seating, so be prepared to eat standing outside or take your order to nearby **Parque Lincoln**. It also makes an easy food stop towards the end of our walking route.
Find more of our favourite taquerías in our guide to **best tacos in Mexico City**.
texts.17:
## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #8 Dine in Style at Pujol (If You’re Planning a Splurge)
Pujol is one of Polanco’s best-known fine-dining restaurants, famous for chef Enrique Olvera’s tasting menus. If a special meal is a priority for your trip, check availability through Pujol’s official website before planning your day around it.
We haven’t eaten here ourselves. We ran out of budget and chose experiences such as the food tour instead, so this is an option to consider rather than a personal dining recommendation.
Check the menu price and what’s included when booking, particularly drinks and any extras. It’s a substantial splurge, but you don’t need a reservation at Pujol to enjoy Polanco: the free museums, parks and casual food stops make a worthwhile visit on their own.
texts.18:
## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #9 Stroll Around Parque Lincoln
Parque Lincoln is the heart of Polanco and one of the nicest places to take a break between museums and shopping. It’s where locals walk their dogs, sit with coffees and bring their kids to play. You don’t need much of an agenda here.
The park has its own aviary, sculptures and two reflecting pools, where we sometimes see people manoeuvring model boats. Those little everyday scenes are part of what we enjoy about wandering around the neighbourhood.
If you’re wondering about the name, the park honours **Abraham Lincoln, who opposed the US invasion of Mexico**. His statue was a gift from President Lyndon Johnson in 1966 and is still on display today.
It’s an easy stop after Pasaje Polanco, with El Turix and several cafés nearby if you’re ready for something to eat.
texts.19:
## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #10 See the Unusual Architecture of St. Augustine Parish Church
A **wonderfully strange, idiosyncratic structure**, the St. Augustine Parish Church was built in 1949 to administer to the spiritual needs of the locals.
Walking towards it from the Parque America, we first thought it looked like a fairly standard religious edifice. As we got closer, though, it became clearer how wonderfully innovative the whole thing is with its almost **industrial-style facade** and a half-dome that has been described by some architecture aficionados as reminiscent of a water tank!
texts.20:
## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #11 Pass Through Parque America
On the way between Old Polanco and Nuevo Polanco, **Parque América** is an easy, pleasant wander, not as iconic as Lincoln, but a nice green break when you’re walking between stops.
We almost always see families here and plenty of dogs, and it’s a good “pause point” before heading back into museums/shopping mode.
texts.21:
## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #12 Take A Photo At Mexico Mi Amor Sign
It might not be on everyone’s list of what to do in Polanco, Mexico City, but getting a snap at the Mexico Mi Amor sign is a fun little **side mission that makes for a stylish Instagram post.**
It’s really a display created by the Tane jewellery store to drum up business, but you don’t have to purchase a diamond-encrusted necklace to take a picture in front of the pinkish-red wall with its green cacti and neon sign.
texts.22:
## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #13 Have Breakfast At El Pendulo Book Store
El Péndulo is one of our favourite **“very CDMX” concepts, a bookstore-meets-café** where you can linger for ages. We usually hang out at the **Condesa** branch, but the Polanco location is just as good, with a terrace that spills onto the street and a cosy, book-lined interior that makes you forget you’re in one of the fanciest parts of the city.
It’s a great stop for breakfast or brunch, especially if you want something more relaxed between museums and shopping. Our usual order is one of the Mexican breakfast plates (their chicken enchiladas in mole are solid), washed down with a big glass of fresh orange juice, plus coffee — and then we inevitably end up browsing books we don’t need.
texts.23:
## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #14 Browse Local Designers at Mercado Escondido (Check Opening Days)
Polanco isn’t really famous for markets, but **Mercado Escondido** is a nice little stop if you’re into local designers, usually a handful of stalls selling things like handmade jewellery, leather goods, and small-batch fashion.
That said, it’s more of a **“nearby bonus stop”** than a must-do, and it can be hit-or-miss depending on the day. We actually showed up once and it was **closed**, so it’s worth checking opening times (or having a backup plan nearby).
texts.24:
## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #15 Read Beside The Lake At Librería Porrúa (Chapultepec)
If you’re doing the Anthropology Museum or spending time in Chapultepec, Librería Porrúa is one of our favourite “slow down” stops. It’s a **bookshop-café with a calm vibe**, perfect for a coffee and a breather after a couple of hours of museums.
If you can, grab a table **beside the lake**. It’s genuinely a lovely place to sit with a drink and decompress, and it feels like a little escape from the city.
texts.25:
## Best Things To Do In Polanco, Mexico City
### #16 See the Sharks at Acuario Inbursa (An Option for Families)
If you’re visiting Polanco with kids, **Acuario Inbursa** is another option near Soumaya and Jumex. Its exhibits include sharks, jellyfish and penguins, offering a change from art museums and shopping.
**We haven’t visited ourselves**, so this is an option to consider rather than a personal recommendation. General admission includes both Acuario Inbursa and the Acuario Interactivo; children under three enter free.
If you’re interested in a penguin encounter, check the separate ticket options and availability before booking, as it isn’t included in standard admission.
*   **TICKETS:** $350 MXN general admission, including Acuario Interactivo  
*   **OPENING HOURS:** Daily, 10 am–6 pm  
*   **BOOKING:**Official tickets and current prices
texts.26:
## Is Polanco Safe?
Polanco is one of the **safest-feeling neighborhoods in Mexico City**, where **we’ve felt most comfortable walking around during the day and early evening**. There’s plenty of activity around the shopping streets, restaurants and hotels, and you’ll notice security around many businesses.
That doesn’t mean you should switch off your usual city awareness. We keep bags zipped, avoid leaving phones on café tables and pay attention to our surroundings when checking directions. Late at night, we prefer taking an Uber back rather than walking along quieter streets.
For a broader, city-wide safety breakdown, see our **Mexico City Safety Guide**
texts.27:
## Best Places To Eat In Polanco
Polanco is known for fine dining, but you don’t have to commit to a tasting menu every time you eat here. We’ve found plenty of places for brunch, seafood and tacos, although restaurant prices generally reflect the neighbourhood.
For more recommendations and details, see our **Polanco restaurants guide**.
texts.28:
## Best Places To Eat In Polanco
### Best Brunch & Dinner Spots in Polanco
These are places we’ve enjoyed for a meal without going down the tasting-menu route. They’re not all budget options, but they offer different ways to eat out here.
**Porter Steakhouse & Seafood** – A good choice for a smart dinner without an overly formal atmosphere. We enjoyed the tuna sashimi, and steaks are a main draw if you eat meat.
**Bellopuerto** – One of our go-to picks for seafood. The shrimp aguachile is excellent, but our favourite is the grilled octopus. It’s a good option for sharing a few dishes.
**Catamundi** – Not cheap, but we think it’s worth considering for brunch. The menu includes bagels, shakshuka and Mexican egg dishes, with cocktails if you’re settling in for a long lunch. Our repeat order is the **flautas ahogadas**, crispy tortillas “drowned” in salsa, cheese and cream. There’s also a little gourmet shop attached.
texts.29:
## Best Places To Eat In Polanco
### Best Coffee Shops & Breakfast
For a café break or a relaxed breakfast, these are three places to consider. You’ll find more recommendations in our **best coffee shops in Mexico City** guide.
**Café Toscano Polanco** – An Italian restaurant that also serves Mexican breakfast dishes such as enfrijoladas, enchiladas and molletes. We like the leafy terrace, while the interior has an eclectic mix of furniture and decorative bits.
**Toulo Café** – A café with a Parisian feel and carefully presented cappuccinos, chai lattes and affogatos. Food options include French toast and avocado toast with a poached egg.
**El Péndulo** – Our bookshop-café pick for breakfast and a leisurely browse. We usually order a Mexican breakfast plate, such as chicken enchiladas in mole, with fresh orange juice and coffee.
texts.30:
## Best Places To Eat In Polanco
### Where to Find the Best Tacos in Polanco
For something more casual, these are the taco spots we’ve tried. **El Turix would be our first choice**, particularly if you want cochinita pibil.
**El Turix** – Our favourite for tacos and panuchos filled with cochinita pibil. There’s no proper seating, so eat standing outside or take your order to nearby Parque Lincoln.
**TAKOS TAKOS** – A practical choice when you want a seat and a break from walking. The menu covers everything from salads to meat plates, but we’d stick with the **arrachera tacos**.
texts.31:
## Polanco Nightlife
Polanco nightlife leans towards smart cocktail bars and clubs where people dress up. It’s not our first choice for a big night out, as we prefer **Roma Norte’s** atmosphere, but it’s convenient if you’re staying nearby and want drinks after dinner.
For cocktails, **Licorería Limantour’s Polanco branch**, on Óscar Wilde near Parque Lincoln, is a good option. We still prefer the Roma location for the overall atmosphere, but we’ve enjoyed the drinks here too.
For a club night, **Vanderbilt Masaryk** and **Kennedy Social Room** are options to consider. Expect a dressier evening rather than a casual café-bar atmosphere, and check directly with the venue about reservations, entry arrangements and the night’s programme before heading over.
For more places to go out across the city, read our **Mexico City nightlife guide**.
texts.32:
## Wrap-Up
For us, Polanco is worth visiting for the free museums, a stroll around Masaryk and Parque Lincoln, and a good meal along the way. Choose the stops that interest you rather than trying to cover everything, especially if you’re also planning to visit Chapultepec.
For ideas beyond the neighbourhood, explore our **best things to do in Mexico City**.

248 We finally made it! We’ve been wanting to check out this market for a while, but we knew it was not going to be your average in and out grocery trip. Most of you know I’m a big foodie, so Northgate’s Mercado González concept is definitely my version of a good time. It’s basically a Mexican food hall and market rolled into one, designed to feel like the traditional mercados in Mexico with more than 20 food stands and pretty much every ingredient you could imagine. Going on a Saturday definitely added to the chaos! We grabbed some tacos dorados to fuel up for shopping and I washed mine down with an agua fresca de mamey. Miché while shopping? Yes please! We watched our churros get fried, picked up tortillas that were literally hot off the press, and wandered the aisles sampling different foods and gathering ingredients for dinner. Mom also wanted to take me to a spot called Fermentation Farm for fresh kombucha. I got myself bottles of my two favorite fruit flavors: guava and passion fruit. I also snagged a fermented sambal that turned into a tangy drizzle for blackened cod and cheesy chile tacos for dinner. I planned this trip home to spend time with my mama and sister with no real agenda. Yesterday was a fun little adventure filled with good food and unhurried wandering, and it was exactly what I needed. What's your favorite cultural market to check out unique eats near you? I'd love some ideas on more places to check out 🙌🏽

248 We finally made it! We’ve been wanting to check out this market for a while, but we knew it was not going to be your average in and out grocery trip. Most of you know I’m a big foodie, so Northgate’s Mercado González concept is definitely my version of a good time. It’s basically a Mexican food hall and market rolled into one, designed to feel like the traditional mercados in Mexico with more than 20 food stands and pretty much every ingredient you could imagine. Going on a Saturday definitely added to the chaos! We grabbed some tacos dorados to fuel up for shopping and I washed mine down with an agua fresca de mamey. Miché while shopping? Yes please! We watched our churros get fried, picked up tortillas that were literally hot off the press, and wandered the aisles sampling different foods and gathering ingredients for dinner. Mom also wanted to take me to a spot called Fermentation Farm for fresh kombucha. I got myself bottles of my two favorite fruit flavors: guava and passion fruit. I also snagged a fermented sambal that turned into a tangy drizzle for blackened cod and cheesy chile tacos for dinner. I planned this trip home to spend time with my mama and sister with no real agenda. Yesterday was a fun little adventure filled with good food and unhurried wandering, and it was exactly what I needed. What's your favorite cultural market to check out unique eats near you? I'd love some ideas on more places to check out 🙌🏽

Qi Yang Chengwei Qin ††thanks: Corresponding to [chengweiqin@hkust-gz.edu.cn](mailto:chengweiqin@hkust-gz.edu.cn)Affiliation:The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) Affiliation:Ant Group

###### Abstract
Training-time multi-agent system (MAS) design seeks to learn reusable orchestration policies, yet prevailing approaches remain largely one-shot: an Orchestrator generates a system but only observes and learns from its terminal outcome. This paradigm discards execution trajectories that expose system-level failures and contain fine-grained information beyond the terminal outcome, leaving no direct basis for revising the source MAS, evaluating the updated MAS, or learning from the resulting contrast. To this end, we introduce MAS-Loop, an execution-grounded framework that closes this feedback loop by coupling an Orchestrator with a trajectory-conditioned Refiner. For each task, the Orchestrator constructs and executes a source MAS to obtain an outcome score and an intermediate trajectory. Conditioned on the trajectory, the Refiner localizes an actionable failure, formulates a trajectory-grounded diagnosis, and proposes a bounded patch to the agents, information flow, or execution configuration. The executable updated MAS is re-executed on the same task to measure its realized outcome under stochastic execution. This pair-MAS comparison provides complementary learning signals: the Orchestrator learns to generate strong systems with fewer recoverable failures, whereas the Refiner learns to expose and repair observed weaknesses, thereby driving policy-level co-evolution across training iterations. We evaluate MAS-Loop across interaction environments, knowledge-intensive multi-hop reasoning, and general reasoning, examining both the complete framework and the independent utility of these two policies. Experiments show that MAS-Loop achieves the strongest overall performance among the evaluated baselines, with consistent gains from refinement across all evaluated benchmarks. The co-evolution process also yields MAS-JudgeCorpus, a dataset of execution-grounded source-updated pairs with orchestration- and trajectory-level supervision, which can provide the community with support for MAS reward modeling and trajectory-aware investigation.

## 1 Introduction
Training-time multi-agent system (MAS) design has emerged as a promising alternative to inference-time MAS design, where the workflow search must be repeated for different tasks and cannot accumulate reusable experience across tasks(Zhang et al., 2025; Ke et al., 2025b; Hu et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026c). Training-time MAS trains an Orchestrator to construct a task-specific MAS by selecting models or tools, assigning agent roles, and organizing communication(Li et al., 2024; Ke et al., 2025a; Tran et al., 2025). The system then executes and uses its outcomes to improve the Orchestrator through supervised learning(Ye et al., 2025; Yue et al., 2025), reinforcement learning(Yang and Thomason, 2026; Ke et al., 2026), and graph-based optimization(Zhuge et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). In this way, experience acquired from previous executions can be encoded into a reusable orchestration policy and transferred to future tasks(Lin et al., 2026d).
Although this makes MAS construction learnable, this _one-shot orchestration_ remains an incomplete foundation for effective MAS self-evolution(Qi et al., 2026): orchestration and execution feedback remain disconnected. A system trajectory can expose missing information flow, redundant reasoning, or failures in verification and aggregation(Shen et al., 2025; Cemri et al., 2026). Yet this trajectory-level evidence is often omitted from the terminal correctness signal(Jwalapuram et al., 2026). Therefore, without a feedback-driven refinement mechanism, the Orchestrator must discover better designs indirectly through independently sampled rollouts and their sparse outcome rewards(Zhang, 2026; Su et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026b; Peng et al., 2026). Although this trial-and-error process may eventually favor stronger systems, it relies on vanilla independent rollouts and sparse terminal rewards rather than utilizing rich intermediate trajectories as feedback to directly diagnose failures, guide targeted repairs, and optimize from verified improvements.

(b) MAS-Loop moves from one-shot orchestration to execution-grounded adversarial co-evolution by adding a trajectory-conditioned Refiner and incorporating coupled incentive learning signals.
However, a complete self-evolution loop requires more than learning to generate the next system: it should connect execution evidence to a direct intervention on the current system and facilitate learning based on the consequences of that intervention(Chen et al., 2026a; Yang et al., 2026a). To this end, we introduce MAS-Loop, an execution-grounded framework that augments the _Orchestrator_ with a complementary learned policy, the _Refiner_. The Orchestrator first constructs a source MAS, whose execution produces a terminal score and an intermediate trajectory. The Refiner observes the source design, final prediction, and trajectory to localize actionable weaknesses, formulate a grounded diagnosis, and propose a bounded patch to agent roles, information flow, or execution settings. This patch is compiled into an updated MAS and re-executed on the same task to measure the realized outcome change. The source-updated score difference provides coupled learning signals: it encourages the Orchestrator to produce strong systems with fewer recoverable weaknesses and trains the Refiner to generate valid revisions that repair observed failures, enabling the two policies to co-evolve from this rich-learning closed-loop. This co-evolution occurs across policy-optimization iterations: each rollout contains one bounded refinement, while subsequent task rollouts use the newly updated Orchestrator and Refiner.
During policy co-evolution, MAS-Loop naturally produces large numbers of execution-grounded source-updated pairs. To obtain reliable comparisons, we retain tasks with a fixed rollout budget, discard ties and pairs with insufficient absolute or relative score gaps, remove locally inconsistent examples, and canonicalize Refiner operations before operation-aware deduplication. The resulting MAS-JudgeCorpus contains source and updated MAS instances whose quality differences are established by same-task re-execution, providing pairwise preferences for training MAS reward models with orchestration- and execution-level supervision. Then we leverage MAS-JudgeRM for test-time ranking and selection among candidate MAS, while the retained trajectory evidence also offers a basis for future trajectory-conditioned judging and other execution-aware evaluations.

## 1 Introduction
We evaluate MAS-Loop across interaction environments, knowledge-intensive multi-hop reasoning, and general reasoning, including both in-task performance and out-of-task transfer. MAS-Loop achieves the strongest overall performance among the evaluated single-agent and automatic MAS baselines. The Orchestrator remains effective independently, while the Refiner consistently improves both its source systems and those produced by other MAS methods across in-task and out-of-task evaluations. For MAS-JudgeCorpus, we train MAS-JudgeRM on pairwise preferences and compare it with general-purpose reward models, orchestration-specific reward models, and prompted LLM judges for selecting among a fixed set of candidate MAS. Together, these experiments assess both MAS-Loop’s effectiveness as a self-evolving MAS framework and MAS-JudgeCorpus’s value for test-time MAS selection. Our contributions are summarized as follows:
*   •  
We identify a central limitation of current training-time MAS: one-shot orchestration leaves execution feedback disconnected from the MAS design, forcing the Orchestrator to improve indirectly through sparse terminal rewards rather than direct rich trajectory-level evidence.

*   •  
We introduce MAS-Loop, an execution-grounded framework that couples an Orchestrator with a trajectory-conditioned Refiner. The paired re-execution evaluates the updated MAS under the same task protocol and provides complementary learning signals that drive both policies to co-evolve across training iterations.

*   •  
We construct MAS-JudgeCorpus from execution-grounded source–updated MAS pairs, applying fixed-rollout quality filtering, conservative consistency checks, and operation-aware deduplication to obtain reliable preferences for training MAS reward models.

## Appendix C Experimental Details
### C.1 Statistics of Benchmarks
Table3 summarizes the role of every benchmark in the experiments. ALFWorld, HotpotQA, and DeepScaler provide the three training resources for interaction environment, multi-hop question answering, and general reasoning, respectively. Their corresponding in-task test sets measure whether the learned policies retain performance in the task family used during training. SciWorld, VitaBench, BrowseComp-Plus, and GPQA-Diamond are held-out out-of-task (OOT) benchmarks and therefore test transfer to a related but distinct task distribution.
Interaction environments.ALFWorld aligns abstract text environments with embodied household tasks, allowing an agent to learn and execute the same high-level task through language actions(Shridhar et al., 2020). Its tasks require long-horizon planning, object manipulation, and adaptation to different household layouts, making it a natural training and in-task evaluation environment for interactive agents. SciWorld requires the agent to inspect objects, perform experiments through sequential actions, and infer the scientific outcome(Wang et al., 2022a). VitaBench evaluates multi-turn tool-using agents in real-world service scenarios, including food delivery, in-store consumption, and online travel(He et al., 2026). It exposes agents to changing user intentions, interdependent tool calls, and dynamic service states, thereby testing practical decision-making and recovery over extended interactions.
Knowledge-intensive QA.HotpotQA is a Wikipedia-based multi-hop question-answering dataset whose questions require combining evidence from multiple documents(Yang et al., 2018). BrowseComp-Plus evaluates deep-research agents over a fixed and curated document corpus, providing a reproducible alternative to evaluation against the continuously changing open web(Chen et al., 2025). Its questions require iterative retrieval, source comparison, and evidence synthesis, which makes it suitable for measuring transfer from standard multi-hop QA to more complex deep-research tasks.

## Appendix D Additional Ablation Experiments
### D.2 One-Step Prompted Self-Reflection
We add a non-learned reflection control to distinguish the contribution of the trained Refiner from the generic benefit of an additional trajectory-conditioned inference pass. Given the task, source MAS, final prediction, and the same gold-free execution trajectory available to MAS-Loop, the Orchestrator is prompted once (i.e., using the self-correction prompt(He et al., 2025)) to diagnose the execution and emit one revision under the same bounded operation interface. The revised MAS is compiled and re-executed once. This control therefore matches the source-revision-re-execution structure but introduces no separately trained Refiner or coupled reward.

## Appendix D Additional Ablation Experiments
### D.3 Base-Model Scaling: Qwen3-14B
We replace Qwen3-8B with Qwen3-14B for both the Orchestrator and Refiner while keeping the task data, policy interfaces, reward definitions, rollout group size, frozen sub-agent backbone, executor, and evaluation protocol unchanged. This comparison tests whether MAS-Loop generalizes to a larger base model and can effectively convert increased policy capacity into improved in-task and out-of-task performance.
Table 5: Ablation results for rollout-execution matching, one-step prompted self-reflection, and base-model scaling.
Analysis.Table5 shows that the default MAS-Loop substantially outperforms rollout-execution-matched MAS-Orchestra on both HotpotQA and BCP. Thus, increasing the number of independently generated and executed MAS rollouts alone does not recover the benefit of trajectory-conditioned refinement. The self-correction results remain below MAS-Loop, isolating the benefit of learning a dedicated Refiner rather than merely prompting for an additional reflection pass. Replacing the trainable policies with Qwen3-14B further improves MAS-Loop on both benchmarks, demonstrating that the framework generalizes across base-model scales and benefits from stronger policy backbones.

## Appendix E Case Study
We show one case from BrowseComp-Plus and compare the MAS produced by Orchestrator and Refiner. The Orchestrator returns Northgate Market, whereas the Refiner rewrote the role of agent_0 to require explicit confirmation of the candidate’s presence in both Mexico and California. This constraint discouraged premature selection based on the salient California event clue alone and promoted a more complete evaluation of the two-location condition. The revised evidence flow consequently preserved Churrería El Moro as the candidate passed to downstream aggregation, thus yielding the correct answer.

BrowseComp-Plus evaluates deep-research agents over a fixed and curated document corpus, providing a reproducible alternative to evaluation against the continuously changing open web(Chen et al., 2025). Its questions require iterative retrieval, source comparison, and evidence synthesis, which makes it suitable for measuring transfer from standard multi-hop QA to more complex deep-research tasks.
texts.50:
## Appendix D Additional Ablation Experiments
### D.2 One-Step Prompted Self-Reflection
We add a non-learned reflection control to distinguish the contribution of the trained Refiner from the generic benefit of an additional trajectory-conditioned inference pass. Given the task, source MAS, final prediction, and the same gold-free execution trajectory available to MAS-Loop, the Orchestrator is prompted once (i.e., using the self-correction prompt(He et al., 2025)) to diagnose the execution and emit one revision under the same bounded operation interface. The revised MAS is compiled and re-executed once. This control therefore matches the source-revision-re-execution structure but introduces no separately trained Refiner or coupled reward.
texts.51:
## Appendix D Additional Ablation Experiments
### D.3 Base-Model Scaling: Qwen3-14B
We replace Qwen3-8B with Qwen3-14B for both the Orchestrator and Refiner while keeping the task data, policy interfaces, reward definitions, rollout group size, frozen sub-agent backbone, executor, and evaluation protocol unchanged. This comparison tests whether MAS-Loop generalizes to a larger base model and can effectively convert increased policy capacity into improved in-task and out-of-task performance.
Table 5: Ablation results for rollout-execution matching, one-step prompted self-reflection, and base-model scaling.
Analysis.Table5 shows that the default MAS-Loop substantially outperforms rollout-execution-matched MAS-Orchestra on both HotpotQA and BCP. Thus, increasing the number of independently generated and executed MAS rollouts alone does not recover the benefit of trajectory-conditioned refinement. The self-correction results remain below MAS-Loop, isolating the benefit of learning a dedicated Refiner rather than merely prompting for an additional reflection pass. Replacing the trainable policies with Qwen3-14B further improves MAS-Loop on both benchmarks, demonstrating that the framework generalizes across base-model scales and benefits from stronger policy backbones.
texts.52:
## Appendix E Case Study
We show one case from BrowseComp-Plus and compare the MAS produced by Orchestrator and Refiner. The Orchestrator returns Northgate Market, whereas the Refiner rewrote the role of agent_0 to require explicit confirmation of the candidate’s presence in both Mexico and California. This constraint discouraged premature selection based on the salient California event clue alone and promoted a more complete evaluation of the two-location condition. The revised evidence flow consequently preserved Churrería El Moro as the candidate passed to downstream aggregation, thus yielding the correct answer.

Title: Eater LA on Instagram: "Grocery chain Northgate (@northgatemarket) is going hard on a marketplace format common in Mexico with upwards of 20 colorful stalls and food options called Mercado Gonzalez, which will include famed El Moro churro stand from Mexico City, carnitas from Carnitas Don Miguel, tortas by Chiva Torta, and tacos by Tacos Los Guichos, available from breakfast through dinner.

Located in the grocer’s new Costa Mesa location and scheduled to open in early November, the food hall and marketplace will take after notable markets like Mercado Juarez in Monterrey, Mercado de Abastos in Guadalajara, and Mercado de Aretesanias in Oaxaca.

The beating heart of Mercado Gonzalez will be a butcher shop, tortilleria, cheese specialist, produce stands, specialty foods, and other artisan goods that one would find in Mexico. The concept itself is a smart reworking of the typical American supermarket layout but with the intuitiveness and walkability of a Mexican mercado.

Click on the link in bio to read more about the soon-to-open Mercado Gonzalez, and to check out some other colorful renderings of the marketplace and food hall. Written by Eater LA lead editor Matthew Kang (@mattatouille).

Renderings by @shookkelley"

Inside Northgate González Market's immersive new 'Mercado'
opened.information:
Source: https://www.grocerydive.com/news/northgate-gonzalez-markets-mercado-store-mexican-cuisine-shook-kelley/700248/
Title: Inside Northgate González Market’s immersive new ‘Mercado’
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
A newly opened store in Costa Mesa, California, aims to flip the traditional grocery shopping experience on its head by immersing consumers in Mexican culture and cuisine.
Mercado González, which opened earlier this month, is a new concept from Northgate González Market that offers up authentic cuisine in food stalls and a Mexican fine-dining restaurant. The store also serves as a celebration of Mexican culture with its vivid and colorful design elements.
Architect Kevin Kelley, whose firm Shook Kelley designed the location, called the recently opened location a “game changer” for the grocery industry.
“The Hispanic/Latin/Mexican market has been underrepresented in terms of grocery stores ... They have never really had the limelight. They have never been celebrated in a big way. They have never really been viewed for the culinary adventure they bring people on,” Kelley said.
Mercado González is aiming to change that with a store that offers “the sights, scents, sounds, and tastes of Mexico,” according to its website.
Permission granted by Robert Sanchez
Permission granted by Robert Sanchez

### **Celebrating a family legacy and Mexican culture**
After a fire destroyed his shoe shop in Jalostotitlán in Jalisco, Mexico, Don Miguel moved to the United States and converted a liquor store into the first Northgate Market, which opened in Anaheim, California, in 1980. The grocery company’s name stems from the combination of the liquor store’s name — Northgate — with the family name.
The chain celebrated its 40th anniversary in 2020. Currently third-generation owned, Northgate has grown to 43 stores, including the newly opened location with the mercado concept.
Initially, the grocery chain focused on the Mexican consumer before broadening its target customer base to non-Mexican Latin and Hispanic shoppers, Kelley said.
By the time the chain started working with Shook Kelley about three years ago, however, its stores had come to look “[more] like a Ralph’s” as the González family sought to model a traditional American supermarket in order to overcome stereotypes surrounding Hispanic grocery stores, Kelley said.
Permission granted by Robert Sanchez
Permission granted by Robert Sanchez
“They’re very aware that sometimes people look at Mexican food as not as high class or as high culinary and they don’t believe that and they don’t like that view,” Kelley said.
Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Grocery Dive free daily newsletter
But Shook Kelley encouraged the chain to embrace its roots and roll out a new concept that serves up authentic Mexican cuisine as a differentiated approach and competitive advantage — leading to the creation of Mercado González, Kelley said. In Mexico, mercados serve as lively gathering spots that host numerous vendors.
“What would a real Mexican culture grocery store look like — the actual idea of a mercado?” was the driving question behind the mercado concept, Kelley said.
While the Los Angeles area has a large Hispanic and Latino population, Mercado González aims to cater to Mexican consumers as well as the broader population diversity in the area, Kelley said.
“I believe it will attract the non-Mexicans to this concept because of its authenticity, just as much as we all love to go to a genuine sushi house or a genuine Thai restaurant,” Kelley said about the newly opened store.
Permission granted by Robert Sanchez
Permission granted by Robert Sanchez

### Cooking up authenticity
Inside Mercado González, shoppers can find more than two dozen puestos— food stalls — that serve up both dine-in and carry-out options.
“You can eat in a market but you can also take your food home,” Kelley said.

Grocery chain Northgate (@northgatemarket) is going hard on a marketplace format common in Mexico with upwards of 20 colorful stalls and food options called Mercado Gonzalez, which will include famed El Moro churro stand from Mexico City, carnitas from Carnitas Don Miguel, tortas by Chiva Torta, and tacos by Tacos Los Guichos, available from breakfast through dinner.

The concept itself is a smart reworking of the typical American supermarket layout but with the intuitiveness and walkability of a Mexican mercado.

A newly opened store in Costa Mesa, California, aims to flip the traditional grocery shopping experience on its head by immersing consumers in Mexican culture and cuisine.
Mercado González, which opened earlier this month, is a new concept from Northgate González Market that offers up authentic cuisine in food stalls and a Mexican fine-dining restaurant. The store also serves as a celebration of Mexican culture with its vivid and colorful design elements.
Architect Kevin Kelley, whose firm Shook Kelley designed the location, called the recently opened location a “game changer” for the grocery industry.
“The Hispanic/Latin/Mexican market has been underrepresented in terms of grocery stores ... They have never really had the limelight. They have never been celebrated in a big way. They have never really been viewed for the culinary adventure they bring people on,” Kelley said.
Mercado González is aiming to change that with a store that offers “the sights, scents, sounds, and tastes of Mexico,” according to its website.
